1. **Chart type**: Scatter plot.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Single-panel chart  
- No faceting or small multiples  
- No stacking  
- Uses direct text labels for selected points and horizontal reference lines/annotations

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Reading time (minutes to read) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Readability score | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Item/source title or website name (e.g., Airbnb, Netflix, BBC, book titles) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to points |
| Category/group distinction (websites/news sources vs books/literary works) | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of points and labels (black vs light gray) |

Visible non-data annotations:
- Horizontal dashed lines mark reading-level reference bands (“High school,” “College,” “Professional career” reading level).
- An arrow/text annotation indicates higher y-values are “Harder to read.”

A Messy-cum-Tricky Graph

At first glance, it seems to provide data regarding the amount of time spent readinng a privacy policy and the readibility of text. 
But if I dig deeper, it could not help us actually compare between any two companies' privacy policy. 
For example, if we take two companies on the graph having nearly same reading time ( Netflix and Reddit) and compare them, they have considerable difference in readibility, which suggests that Netlix's would be harder to read than Reddit. So, if reading Netflix's is hard, it should take more time to read than Reddit given the fact that both of them have same reading minutes.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of the surveyed businesses have privacy policies with a readability score above 1300. A reading score of 1300 marks the beginning of the college level complexity range. 

I wonder why the majority of these corporations’ privacy policies are written in a more complex manner that’s more difficult to comprehend from the perspective of a consumer. As a high school consumer of these services, I feel that it is necessary to possess a genuine understanding of my data and how it’s used and distributed. However, due to my current educational background, this understanding I desire is likely much harder for me to grasp in comparison to a college student or professor capable of reading at this level. Ironically, only 33% of Americans over the age of 25 have a college degree that would enable them to do so. It is no secret that there are far less Americans who have graduated college than those who have. So then why would these corporations choose to make their privacy policies so strenuous?

Corporations take advantage of the uneducated public to hide their true intentions “stated” in their privacy policies.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that the graph depicts the level of difficulty in reading the privacy policies of websites. I’ve noticed that most big corporations use difficult language at a professional level in their policies. I’ve also noticed that most of these companies have policies that take 20-40 minutes to read.  This is because the high reading level makes it difficult for people to understand the policies, so it takes them longer to read. I wonder how they collected this information? Were people asked to read these policies for an experiment, and if so, how many people were taken into account ? I’ve also noticed that the books that were compared to these policies are usually books that are taught in high school. Most of these books are old, so the diction is very difficult, and most people struggle to comprehend these books . However, this graph shows that these texts were easier to read than most of the privacy policies for big companies. So, I think  this graph is attempting to convey the message that big corporations use difficult diction in their policies to scam people into quickly subscribing or using their website/app. Most people will tend to quickly skim over the policies, due to the difficult language, because it’s not likely they would spend 20-40 minutes reading and comprehending this information. These policies could contain loopholes or risks involved in that app that people won’t be able to recognize and may regret later when a problem occurs within the website/app.

comments.raw_comment: The graph, at first glance shows the difficulty of reading certain companies privacy policies. As someone who is familiar with certain businesses presented on the graph, I have never read one privacy policy. As consumers, we want to continue on the app, skipping through the “boring” agreements when we first purchase the app. Companies known for presenting news stories are seen towards the middle with the privacy policy taking 15-20 minutes to read. I believe the time taken to read the policy serves importance as it shows what type of companies may take longer to read. Certain social media apps are in the high school and college average lexile reading range, these apps are appealing to consumers. They wouldn’t put their policies in a professional career reading level if teenagers would skim the policy in the first place. I am curious what the dots not emphasized represent, other businesses? I am also curious why a popular app such as airbnb which can be used by anyone would have a such high reading level. Some consumers of the app may have not received high education and wouldn’t know how to comprehend the privacy policy. Businesses should appeal to the consumer. One can infer that companies towards the bottom of the reading level may be used by everyday people, such as “Amazon” or “home depot”. In my opinion, the deeper meaning is companies should appeal to their consumers.

comments.raw_comment: This graph is set up in a way that compares website and app privacy policies’ difficulty and how long they take to read. The first thing I noticed was that many social media pages share similar reading levels, though some take longer to read than others. The next thing I noticed was that larger companies or news sites typically had a much higher readability score than the rest of the graph, yet remained in a medium area for how much time it took to read. There are also popular novels in more faded texts, likely placed to help guide a viewers understanding of the difficulty of each policy. I do wonder what the other smaller dots are meant to represent, although I am guessing that they are smaller name companies or apps. I believe that the deeper story within this graph is to show how the larger companies typically use more confusing or higher level writing, which may confuse or put off the reader from completely analyzing the policies, as shown in larger companies like GoDaddy, Walt Disney, CNN, and CNS Sports. Their reading levels are higher yet time taken to read is low, likely due to readers skimming long privacy policies instead of taking the time to struggle through the more difficult writing. Whether intentional or not, these companies show an odd ratio between difficulty and time taken to read, while social media companies like Snapchat and Reddit maintain a medium difficulty with a medium time taken to read.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that most companies use very advanced language in their privacy policies, with the majority at a college reading level or higher. Considering that 2% of Americans actually have a college reading level, it seems apparent that either the readability of these policies is not considered—this could cause things like legal jargon to muddle things—or companies deliberately use impregnable language to obfuscate the content of their policies.

I wonder why companies use such inaccessible language in agreements which they expect everyone to read. Are they trying to conceal otherwise unacceptable terms in a shroud of verbosity so that they might slip past the consumer unnoticed?

comments.raw_comment: When I look at this graph, I immediately notice that one of the highest readability privacy policies is for CNN. As displayed on the right side of the graph, CNN is depicted as having a professional career reading level. It also has a somewhat mild reading time. This gives me the idea that higher-level media are more viewed by higher leveled readers due to the fact that it may be more appealing to them. I then look over to things like Snapchat and Reddit and see that they are at a lower reading score. Things like these are commonly seen in use by children and or teens. They also have lower reading times making me think that depending upon the reading material or category of these media, the details in privacy policies change. For example, the app Airbnb has the highest reading time of all data displayed. This may be because of the realm of appeal this app is in is more complex. Airbnb is a system used to book hotel stays. This means that more complex applications like these have more conditional statements for things like policies in a hotel. All of this makes me wonder whether or not developers of these privacy policies pay attention to their target audiences when making them. For example, if social media is targeted towards young audiences, privacy policies should be shorter and at a lower reading level to best appeal to teens. The graph shows higher reading times for these media, however, which is surprising to me. I would name this graph "Privacy Policies: Time to Read?"

Are Netflix and Facebook writing privacy policies at college reading levels because their intended audience is people in college or of a general college 'age'?
